newsitem.title: FRANCE: Moslem admits 1994 Morocco attacks at Paris trial.
newsitem.headline: Moslem admits 1994 Morocco attacks at Paris trial.

text.p: A Moslem extremist admitted in a Paris court on Wednesday that he ordered attacks in Morocco including one in which two Spanish tourists died in 1994.
Moroccan Abdelilah "Rachid" Ziyad, 38, said he recruited and trained Islamic guerrilla groups in France and ran shipments of arms to Algerian Moslem militants via France and Morocco.

"I appealed to Islam, to religion," Ziyad told the court of his recruitment methods in depressed French suburbs. The trial is under tight guard after a bomb on a Paris train by suspected Algerian Moslem extremists killed four people last week.

Taking the stand on the third day of the trial, Ziyad said he set up networks in Paris and in the suburb of La Courneuve. He said Mohamed "Said" Zinedine, a fellow Islamist on trial in his absence, recruited in the towns of Orleans and Besancon.

Some of the 33 other defendants, all formally accused of criminal conspiracy in connection with a terrorist enterprise, have accused Ziyad and Zinedine of indoctrinating them at holiday-like breaks in the French countryside.
Ziyad surprised the court by admitting his leading role and by saying that he organised four attacks in Morocco in 1994.

Two Spanish tourists were shot dead in one of the attacks, a robbery of a Marrakesh hotel. In another, the guerrillas had a gunfight with police in Fez. He did not deny that other abortive attacks targeted Jews in Casablanca and "nudists" at Tangier.
Only 21 of the 34 accused were in the dock. Six others, including three French passport holders, are held in Morocco, three of them awaiting execution and the three others serving life terms.

Ziyad said he sent recruits to Afghanistan or Algeria for training in using weapons and explosives. He declined to say how he won financing, saying merely the arms shipments went to the armed wing of Algeria's outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS).
Prosecutors say the guerrillas were recruited by Morocco's outlawed Islamic Youth Movement whose aim was to overthrow King Hassan and set up an Islamic government.
"It was to stir the Moroccan people, make them rise up against a regime known for its despotism," Ziyad said. "The only language that Hassan II's government understands is force."

The 21 in the dock were rounded up in France, many of them in crackdowns after a wave of bomb attacks in France by Algerian Moslem militants in 1995 in which eight people died and more than 160 were injured.

Investigators suspect the Algerian Armed Islamic Group (GIA), which claimed responsibility for last year's bombs, also planted last week's bomb that killed four people and injured almost 100 at the Port-Royal station.
The GIA accuses France of backing Algiers' military authorities in a war that has claimed 50,000 lives since the government scrapped 1992 elections that fundamentalist candidates were poised to win.

French police on Wednesday freed the last two of 14 people seized in raids on Algerian Moslem targets around Paris on Tuesday in a crackdown after last year's bomb attacks. The other 12 were released on Tuesday.
